title: How to Knit a Proper Swatch: The Secret to Machine Knitting Success

chunks.text: Knitting a proper swatch is the key to success with your knitting machine.
Follow along as I knit a swatch.
This is my LK 150 and I'm knitting stockinette, but the process is the same
for all machines and stitch patterns.
Here are suggestions for stitch and row counts.
No matter how you plan to measure your gauge either using a regular
ruler or gauge rulers.
You will be measuring a specific number of stitches and rows within a larger piece.
Measuring within a larger piece allows for accurate measurement without
the distortion of the edges.
Here are some suggestions.
If you're using gauge rulers for a blue ruler cast on 30 stitches.
This would be maybe for a bulky machine.
For a green ruler cast on 60 stitches for a standard machine.
For the yellow ruler cast on 50 stitches for a mid gauge machine.
Of course, you could cast on a 100 stitches and knit a 100 rows as long as
you have more stitches and rows than you're going to be measuring.
Use the cast on method of your choice.
Just get some stitches on the machine.
I pulled every other needle and worked an e wrap cast on over every other needle.
Next, thread the carriage.
Wiggle and pull to confirm that it's threaded correctly.
The yarn is not hung up and it will flow smoothly.
When you are sure that the carriage is threaded correctly
pull down on the working yarn in the back to take up any slack.
You can hang your cast on comb now.
I knit 1 row first and then added my cast on comb and a single weight.
Knit a few rows and end with the carriage on the right.
Remove the working yarn from the carriage, but don't break it or cut it. Just
loop it over the edge of the machine.
Thread up a contrasting color of similar weight and wiggle and pull to confirm that
it is threaded in the carriage correctly.
If not, you run the risk of dropping all the stitches off the machine.
Now I like to hang a clothespin or a chip clip to add some weight
to the tail of yarn.
Knit 2 rows with the contrasting yarn.
Break that waste yarn and secure it with the clip.
Using the clip ensures that the end stitches knit well.
Set your row counter to 000.
Re thread the main yarn in the carriage, wiggle and pull to make sure
that that yarn is inserted correctly and if you need to, reach back
and pull down to take up any slack.
Knit a few rows and place some markers.
Markers are just a short piece of contrasting color yarn
created with a slip knot.
Knit to the row where you want the marker.
The markers will isolate the number of stitches you'll be measuring.
For example, I'm going to be measuring 30 stitches.
So I'll place my marker on needles number 16 left and 16 right.
This isolates the center 30 stitches.
To place a marker put the loop of the marker in the hook of the needle.
Pull out the needle so the stitch falls behind the latch and then pull
the marker through the stitch. Stitch.
In other words, manually knit a stitch with the marker loop.
Do this on both sides.
Then continue knitting the number of rows you'll be measuring.
Remove the main yarn from the feeder but don't cut it.
Loop it around the end of your machine.
Then thread up the contrasting yarn again and knit 2 rows.
Remember to wiggle and pull to make sure the carriage is threaded correctly.
We don't want everything dropping off the machine.
Knit 2 marker rows with the waste yarn and break that contrasting color.
Re thread the main yarn, wiggle and pull and knit 2 or 3 rows.
Next, we'll mark our swatch with the number of our carriage tension.
I'm using tension 6 so I'll create 6 eyelets so I have
a permanent record of the tension.
To make an eyelet, use your single prong transfer tool and remove
a stitch to the tool.
Transfer that stitch to its neighbor.
You'll empty the needle.
Skip a needle and repeat across for the number of eyelets that you need.
Be sure to put all those empty needles back into working position.
We want to just create some eyelets but continue knitting.
On the LK150 and some other machines you can set up
the tension dial to somewhere between 6 and 7 for example.
I might have used 6.5 or 6+.
In that case, I would put 6 eyelets, skip a few needles and then
add an additional eyelet.
Establish a code for yourself, whatever works, so you can see exactly the
setting if you look a few months later.
After you form all your eyelets please be sure to make sure all your
needles are in working position.
Knit a few more rows and then bind off.
I'm using my favorite bind off.
I'm manually knitting that last row with fairly large loops.
Put the yarn in the hooks of the needles and manually knit each 1 of the stitches.
To prepare for the bind off, carefully pull all the needles all the way out.
I'll pull loop through loop to bind off.
Use whatever bind off method you like.
Swatches are a great opportunity to learn and practice different bind
off and cast on methods.
Use the tail of yarn to finish off the last stitch.
With the swatch off the machine and the ends secure you can now wash your
swatch, block it and use whatever methods you'll be using for your finished garment.
This is called dressing your swatch.
It's a good time to discover how the yarn behaves.
Now don't measure your swatch right off the machine.
Let it rest at least 24 hours then dress it.
You might want to let it rest a little bit again.
Your next step is to use a regular ruler or a gauge ruler to establish your gauge.
I suggest attaching a string tag to record your machine, tension,
gauge, dressing method, and any other notes about your swatch.
Knitting a proper swatch is the secret to successful machine knitting.
